Love Waxing Cold
luhv WAKS-ing kohld
phrase
From the Olivet Discourse, Matthew 24:12, where Christ foretells that the love of many shall wax cold.

📖 Biblical Definition

Love waxing cold is the Lord’s solemn prophecy in the Olivet Discourse concerning the days before His coming: And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold. To wax cold is to grow chill, as a fire dies down; and the love spoken of is that fervent love to God and to the brethren which marks the true disciple. The Lord foretells that as iniquity abounds—as lawlessness multiplies, deceivers arise, and tribulation presses—the love of many professors will cool, their first ardor fading into formality, indifference, and self-love. It is a chilling word, for it speaks not of the world’s coldness, which is no surprise, but of the cooling of love among those who once seemed warm. Yet the Lord adds the promise that holds the faithful: But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. The prophecy is therefore both warning and comfort: warning against the deadening effect of abounding sin upon the heart’s love, and the call to watchfulness lest our own love grow cold; comfort in the assurance that true grace perseveres, and that the enduring love of the elect shall not finally fail. The dictionary honors this saying as a searching word for a lawless age, a summons to keep the fire of love burning, and a call to the perseverance by which the saints are kept.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Christ’s prophecy that as iniquity abounds the love of many shall wax cold; a warning to watchfulness, with the promise that he who endures to the end shall be saved.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The saying is treated as mere ancient pessimism or ignored amid abounding sin; Christ warns against cooling love and calls the saints to watchful perseverance.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption is the dismissal of the saying as mere ancient pessimism, or the failure to heed it amid abounding iniquity. The Lord’s word is precise and searching: it speaks not of the cold world, whose hostility is expected, but of the cooling of love among professors—the dying down of a fire once warm, as lawlessness multiplies and tribulation presses. To ignore this is to be unwatchful precisely where the danger lies.

The principle to recover is twofold: the deadening power of abounding sin upon love, and the perseverance of true grace. Where iniquity abounds, the love of many waxes cold (Matt 24:12); even a true church may leave her first love (Rev 2:4), and so the disciple is called to watchfulness, to consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works (Heb 10:24), and to keep the fire burning lest his own love grow chill. Yet the saying ends in hope: he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved (Matt 24:13). The love that perseveres is the mark of the elect, kept by the power of God; the warning drives the saint to watch, and the promise assures him he shall be kept.
